lead: The first Friday after Pentecost is kept in our Church as Golden Friday. It recalls the first sign of the apostles that Acts tells in detail after the Spirit came: Peter and John at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and Peter's words, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you.” The Epistle names the gift that is worth more than gold: love, without which tongues, prophecy and even martyrdom are nothing. The Gospel warns of riches that make it hard to enter the kingdom, and promises that “for God all things are possible”. Today is also the memory of St Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine.

The three readings answer one question: what does the Church really have to give? Not silver and gold, but the name of Jesus, the love poured out by the Spirit, and the treasure of the kingdom that only God can open to us. The key words are the name, love and possible.

r.h: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk
set: Acts 2 ends with a picture of the first community in Jerusalem: devoted to the apostles' teaching, the breaking of bread and the prayers, and going to the temple together day by day (2:42–46). Many “wonders and signs” were done by the apostles (2:43), and chapter 3 now tells one of them at length. The first believers still prayed in the temple with their fellow Jews; faith in Jesus did not mean leaving the God of Israel.

The ninth hour, three in the afternoon, was the time of the evening sacrifice and of prayer in the temple. No other ancient source calls a gate “the Beautiful Gate”. Many identify it with the great bronze gate on the east side of the inner courts, but its place is not certain.
str: vv. 1–3: Peter and John go up to pray; the lame man asks for alms.
vv. 4–5: “Look at us”: he expects money.
v. 6: “I have no silver or gold”: the name of Jesus.
vv. 7–8: Peter raises him up; he walks and leaps and praises God.
vv. 9–10: the people recognize him and are filled with wonder.
¶ Peter's sermon follows at once (3:11–26): “by faith in his name, his name itself has made this man strong” (3:16).
kw: In the Bible the name stands for the person and his power. The apostles do not heal by their own power or holiness (3:12) but in the name of Jesus. The name given by the angel, Yeshua, means “the Lord saves”.
The verb used for the Resurrection of Jesus. The healing of a man lame from birth is a small Easter: the risen Lord raises up one who had never walked.
Isaiah promised for the day of God's coming: “then the lame shall leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). Luke lets us hear that the promise is being kept.
vv: Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
The man was used to people hurrying past. Before any miracle there is a look. Charity begins by seeing the person.
I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.
Peter is not ashamed to be poor. He gives what he has received. The man asked for a coin and received his life back.
And he took him by the right hand and raised him up; and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.

Luke, whom Paul calls “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), notes the feet and ankles. Peter does with his hand what Jesus once did for Peter's mother-in-law: “took her by the hand and lifted her up” (Mark 1:31).
he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
The man who sat outside the gate every day now goes in with the apostles to pray. The first thing he does with his new strength is to praise God.
ch: The Church sees in this scene what she is meant to be. She must care for the poor, and she does. But first she gives what she has received, the name and the life of Jesus. The Catechism teaches that after the Resurrection it is the name of Jesus that fully shows the power of God (CCC 434; see Acts 3:16). A well-known story tells that a pope once showed St Thomas Aquinas the treasures of the Church and said, “The Church can no longer say, ‘Silver and gold I have none.’” Thomas answered, “Neither can she say, ‘Rise and walk.’” The story may be a legend, but it has been told for centuries because it makes the point well.

r.h: If I do not have love, I am nothing
set: In chapters 12–14 Paul answers the Corinthians' questions about spiritual gifts. Some prized speaking in tongues above everything else. Paul has just said that the Church is one body with many members, each with its own gift (12:12–31). Before he gives rules for using the gifts (chapter 14), he shows them “a still more excellent way” (12:31).
This chapter is often read at weddings, and it fits them well. But Paul first wrote it for a quarrelling community, to show what gives every gift its worth.
str: vv. 1–3: without love, tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice are nothing.
vv. 4–6: what love does and does not do.
¶ The reading stops at v. 6. The chapter goes on: love “bears all things” and “never ends” (13:7–8), and of faith, hope and love, “the greatest of these is love” (13:13).
kw: The New Testament's chosen word for the love that God has shown in Christ, the love that “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). It is not first a feeling but a way of acting for the good of the other.

Literally “is long-tempered”, slow to anger. In the Greek Old Testament the same family of words describes God himself: “slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6). Patient love is God's own way with us.
vv: If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.
Corinth was famous for its bronze work. A gong makes a great noise and has nothing inside. The most beautiful speech without love is only noise.
If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

Textual note: the Greek manuscripts differ here by a single letter. Some read “so that I may boast”, which the NRSV follows; others read “to be burned”, which many older translations follow, as does the POC. Either way, even the greatest sacrifice without love gains nothing.
Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant
Paul describes love by verbs, by what it does. Several things that love is not are faults he has already named in the Corinthians: jealousy (3:3) and arrogance (4:18; 5:2).
it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth.
Love is not softness about evil. It cannot be glad when wrong is done, even to an enemy. It is glad when the truth comes out.
ch: The Catechism calls charity the theological virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbour as ourselves for the love of God (CCC 1822). It quotes this chapter at length and calls charity the form of all the virtues (CCC 1825–1827). St Augustine, preaching on the First Letter of John, gave his famous saying, “Love, and do what you will”: if the root of love is within, nothing but good can grow from it (Homilies on 1 John 7.8, in substance). He did not mean that anything goes. He meant that true love of God shapes every act, even correction.

r.h: For God all things are possible
set: Just before this a rich young man asked Jesus what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Jesus told him to keep the commandments, and then to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow him. “When the young man heard this word, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions” (19:22). Today's Gospel is what Jesus says to the disciples as the young man walks away.
str: vv. 23–24: hard for the rich: the camel and the needle.
vv. 25–26: “Then who can be saved?” For God all things are possible.
vv. 27–29: Peter: we have left everything; the twelve thrones and the hundredfold.
v. 30: the first will be last, and the last first.
kw: The largest animal in the land, through the smallest opening. It is a deliberate exaggeration, a way of saying “impossible”. The story of a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye has no ancient evidence behind it, and it softens a saying that Jesus meant to startle.

Literally “new birth”. Here it means the renewal of the whole creation at the end, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory. The same word is used of Baptism in Titus 3:5, “the water of rebirth”.
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
Jesus does not say that the rich are worse than others. He says that riches can hold the heart so tightly that it cannot pass through the narrow door.
Then who can be saved?
In much of the Old Testament wealth was seen as a sign of God's blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14). If even the rich find it so hard, the disciples think, what hope is there for anyone?
For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.
The answer is not that salvation is easy, but that it is God's gift. The angel said the same to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will inherit eternal life.
“For my name's sake”: the same name that healed the lame man in Acts. Mark adds that the hundredfold comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30).
ch: The Church does not condemn wealth as such, but she warns that riches can seize the heart. The Catechism teaches that Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and that detachment from riches is necessary for entrance into the Kingdom (CCC 2544). It teaches that the goods of creation are meant for the whole human race (CCC 2402–2406) and speaks of the Church's love of preference for the poor (CCC 2448). St Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise on this Gospel, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved?, teaching that what must be given up is the soul's clinging to wealth, so that riches may serve others (in substance).

qa: Why is it called Golden Friday?

The name comes from Peter's words, “I have no silver or gold.” The apostles had no gold to give, and what they gave was richer than gold. In our tradition this first Friday after Pentecost honours that first great sign of the apostles after the Spirit came.
Is the hundredfold a promise of wealth?

No. Mark's version says it comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30). It is the new family of the Church: brothers, sisters and mothers in faith, homes opened in hospitality, and above all eternal life. The fishermen who left their nets received the whole Church as their family.
Does 1 Corinthians 13 mean that faith matters less than love?

No. Paul says that faith, hope and love all abide (13:13). Love is the greatest because it alone remains in heaven, where faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled. Faith without love is dead, and love is the life of faith (CCC 1814–1815, 1826).
rite: Golden Friday belongs to the first week of the season of Pentecost in our calendar. It sets the healing at the Beautiful Gate at the start of the season of Pentecost, as a sign that the Spirit has been given for the healing of the world. Today the Eastern Churches also honour St Helena, with her son Constantine. Helena, a woman of humble birth, became the mother of the first Christian emperor. In her old age, around 326–328, she went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and churches were built at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. From the end of the fourth century writers such as St Ambrose told that she found the Cross of the Lord in Jerusalem (in substance). She is a fitting saint for Golden Friday: an empress who used her wealth to honour the places of the Lord's life and to help the poor.
study: Peter said, “what I have I give you.” What have I received from God that I could give to someone today, apart from money?
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–6 and put my own name in place of “love”. Which line is hardest to say truthfully?
What possession or comfort holds my heart most tightly? What would it mean to trust that “for God all things are possible”?
St Helena used her wealth for the Lord's places and the poor. How does our family decide what to give?
